extracted.intended_audience: judicial branch employees, judges, law clerks, patent practitioners, and students seeking an introduction to U.S. patent law and practice
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive introductory guide to United States patent law and practice covering PTO prosecution, patentability standards, litigation (infringement and defenses), remedies, and procedural device such as reexamination, reissue, and appeals. Intended to explain the legal standards and practical rules used by courts, the PTO, and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Three types of patents can be obtained: utility, plant, and design; utility patents are for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (or improvements), plant patents for distinct new varieties of plant, design patents for new, original and ornamental designs for an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monograph focuses on utility patents; terms and maintenance fees differ by type (e.g., design patents 14-year term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent components
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility patent consists of a cover page listing administrative information, a written description (specification and drawings), and one or more claims that define the metes and bounds of the exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover page includes abstract and representative drawing; claims set the owner's exclusive rights; the specification must enable public practice after expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable and disclose best mode (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description must be full, clear, concise, and exact enough to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention and must disclose the best mode known to the inventor at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes discussion of drawings, preferred embodiment, and manufacturing procedures; failure affects validity (enablement, written description, best mode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must 'particularly and distinctly' define invention (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must particularly and distinctly define the subject matter regarded as the invention; they set the metes and bounds of the patent owner's exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims can be independent, dependent, or multiple dependent; drafting skill is critical; punctuation rule: one period only at end of the claim sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant as lexicographer / claim term definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor and drafter may act as their own lexicographer and give words uncommon meanings, but the application must define words used in an uncommon manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain words retain fixed legal effect (e.g., 'comprising' = open, 'consisting of' = closed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope (broad vs narrow) and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims vary in scope: broad claims include fewer limitations and cover broader subject matter; claims are often arranged from broadest to narrowest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent claims for self-contained scope and dependent claims to add limitations and fallback positions; multiple dependent claims refer back to two or more claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function and product-by-process claim treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim formats—means-plus-function and product-by-process—have special rules for interpretation and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function governed by statute/case law (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6); product-by-process claims claim product by the process of making it and have particular claim construction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are required only when necessary to understand the invention; formal rules govern acceptability (e.g., color drawings require petition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs generally not accepted except in limited cases (plant patents sometimes accept color photos). Official draftsman checks formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing requirements and filing date rules (35 U.S.C. §111)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonprovisional application that can mature into a patent consists of a specification, drawings if necessary, an oath/declaration, and required filing fees; the filing date is when the specification and drawings (if necessary) and at least one claim are received (or deposited by Express Mail under certain conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain formal defects can be corrected later (possibly with fees); provisional applications have different (lesser) requirements and are not examined or maturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or declaration contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath/declaration must be signed by the actual inventor(s) and state that the signer has reviewed the specification, believes they are the original and first inventor of the claimed subject matter, and acknowledges the duty to disclose material information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor dead/incapacitated or refuses to sign, limited alternatives exist under rules (37 C.F.R.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and disclosure (37 C.F.R. §1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants, attorneys, and agents are held to a high ethical standard to disclose known material information (duty of candor and good faith); materiality defined in section 1.56(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material information is noncumulative and either establishes a prima facie case of unpatentability or refutes/inconsistent with an applicant position; breach can give rise to inequitable conduct, an equitable defense to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner search and quality factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner conducts a prior art search using examiner's private materials, the examining group's library, and the PTO Scientific Library; quality depends on examiner skill, time allocated, and completeness of libraries searched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References found are recorded on the file wrapper; thoroughness affects prosecution/outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction/election requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application claims more than one invention, the examiner can require restriction (inventions clearly different) or election of species (related inventions with generic claim); applicant must elect one invention for prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-elected inventions, applicant may file divisional applications; election requirement can affect prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation, continuation-in-part, and divisional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may file continuation, continuation-in-part, or divisional applications to pursue non-elected claims or to continue prosecution with altered claim scope or added subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuations keep the benefit of earlier filing dates for common subject matter; CIPs add new matter with different priority consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue and reexamination procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Issued patents can be corrected via reissue (including broadening reissue with intervening rights implications) or reexamined by the PTO to strengthen patents in light of prior art; reexamination has its own standards and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue and reexamination interact with litigation (intervening rights, certificate of reexamination) and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship and assignment formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must be made in the name of the inventor(s); errors in naming (misjoinder/nonjoinder) can often be corrected, but intentional misjoinder/nonjoinder can render a patent invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments are recorded; assignees can be involved in PTO actions. Limited exceptions exist when inventor cannot sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter includes machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, and processes; court decisions (e.g., Chakrabarty, Diehr) have recognized broad scope including microorganisms and certain computer-related inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility, novelty, and nonobviousness remain additional conditions; certain categories like printed matter have special treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be new; anticipation analysis considers prior art (printed publications, patents, use, sale), doctrine of inherency, dates, and whether knowledge was secret/abandoned/suppressed/concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed publication evidentiary rules (including handwritten/oral/publication date) and foreign priority issues affect novelty; statutory sections differ (102(a),(b),(e),(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars: on-sale, public use, printed publication, abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Various statutory bars can defeat patentability: offers for sale/on-sale bar, public use, printed publication, and abandonment prior to statutory cutoff periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-sale bar policies include experimental use exceptions and on-hand requirement; public use bar has burden and policy considerations; secret commercial use can still trigger bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must not be obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art considering scope and content of prior art, differences, and objective/secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, copying, praise, unexpected results, nexus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hindsight; evaluate level of ordinary skill, combination of references; secondary considerations can rebut prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description adequate to show the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter (distinct from enablement though related).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims cannot claim new matter beyond the original disclosure; 'new matter' added during prosecution is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation; timing and level of detail matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include the skill level in the field, predictability, and whether manufacturing procedures are disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor must disclose the best mode of carrying out the invention known at time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose best mode may render a patent unenforceable; discuss within the detailed description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history and prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements and amendments made during prosecution form the prosecution history and can estop the patentee from later asserting claim scope under doctrines like prosecution history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments narrowing claims for patentability reasons can limit doctrine of equivalents scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement and doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement can be literal (accused product/practice meets all claim limitations) or under the doctrine of equivalents (accused product/function is equivalent despite not literally meeting limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests include function-way-result and hypothetical claim analyses; range/reverse doctrine of equivalents and limits exist; prosecution history estoppel can restrict equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement: inducement and contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement includes inducement (active steps to cause infringement) and contributory infringement (selling a component with knowledge and no substantial noninfringing use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge and intent elements are important; contributory requires lack of substantial noninfringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of proof for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove infringement, plaintiff must show (direct) acts such as making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing the patented invention in the U.S.; for process patents, additional rules govern product made by the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial limits (imports), process patent rules, and statutory exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Issued patents enjoy a presumption of validity; burden and standard when challenging validity in court (e.g., clear and convincing evidence) and deference to PTO determinations are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior adjudications, reexamination, and evidence presented in adversarial proceedings may bear on outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses (inequitable conduct, unclean hands, laches, estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several equitable defenses can defeat enforcement of a patent: inequitable conduct (intent to mislead + materiality), unclean hands, laches (delay and prejudice), equitable estoppel (misleading conduct, reliance, prejudice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequitable conduct requires clear and convincing evidence; laches and estoppel have specific elements (material prejudice, reliance, misleading conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies: injunctions (preliminary and permanent) factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider factors for preliminary and permanent injunctions: irreparable harm, balance of hardships, public interest, and likelihood of success (for preliminary); reasons exist for denying permanent injunctions in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trend and history affect injunctive relief; stays and bonding issues may arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies: monetary damages—lost profits and reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners may recover monetary damages including lost profits (Panduit test: demand, absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes, capacity to meet demand, amount of profit) or reasonable royalties (Georgia-Pacific factors/hypothetical negotiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entire market value rule, convoyed sales, incremental costs, market-share analyses, timing of hypothetical negotiation impact damages calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking and notice prerequisite to damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Marking or actual notice can be prerequisites to recovering certain damages; timing and correctness of notice/marking affect available damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory and case-law doctrines (actual notice, marking) discussed; failure may limit recovery to post-notice damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased damages and willful infringement factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may award increased (enhanced) damages for willful infringement; analysis considers factors such as the accused infringer's conduct, competence of opinions, and whether there was an affirmative duty to investigate infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards and required findings (e.g., willfulness) discussed; punitive element considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney fees / exceptional case
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney fees may be awarded to the prevailing party in 'exceptional cases' under governing statutes; determining factors include litigation misconduct, frivolousness, and other equitable considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculation (lodestar) and standards for exceptional case analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction, venue, and appeals (Federal Circuit role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent cases involve federal jurisdiction (arising under), special venue statutes for patent defendants, and appeals to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit to promote national uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue tests for corporate defendants, multiple-patent suits, and patent-specific statutes are relevant; Federal Circuit has wide influence on law and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO procedural devices: protest, interview, appeal to Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may file protests, conduct interviews with examiners, and appeal adverse examiner actions to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (and ultimately to federal courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interferences (priority contests) handled by the Board; oral hearings and notices of allowability/allowance procedures exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority, foreign priority, and international procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority rules govern filing dates, including foreign priority claims and use of Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and provisional applications for priority benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional applications provide a priority date but do not mature into patents; GATT/NAFTA/other treaty implementations affect terms and filing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative formalities and fee rules (small entity reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees vary by claim number and form; small entities (individual inventors, nonprofits, small businesses) may receive fee reductions (e.g., 50%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees are incurred for late arrival of components; filing/issue/maintenance fees and fee strategies affect prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO classification and file wrapper recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO assigns applications to classes/subclasses and art units; the file wrapper contains the prosecution history and references searched and found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification determines examiner/art unit assignment and search scope; file wrapper is important evidence in litigation and prosecution-history analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-filing practices: documenting conception and reduction to practice and prior-art searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Before filing, inventors often document conception and reduction to practice and may conduct prior-art searches (optional but common).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searches may be performed by professional searchers in the PTO Public Search Room; lack of a pre-filing search does not preclude filing but affects strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting formalities and drafting advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be drafted with attention to form (one period at end), choice of open vs closed claim language ('comprising' vs 'consisting of'), and a hierarchy of claims from broad to narrow; skilled claim-drafting resources and treatises exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims drafting is a specialized skill; many reference texts and training exist; changes in number/form of claims can trigger fees and prosecution consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory term and term adjustments/extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term rules changed (e.g., GATT-implementing legislation): term ends twenty years from filing (with possible adjustments/extensions); maintenance fees and potential extensions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional rules and the effect of earlier filing dates/applications may modify term; reissue/reexamination can affect term and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial management and juror comprehension in patent jury trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents raise special jury considerations: juror comprehension of technical evidence, the jurors' role, form of verdict, and instructions; courts can manage trials to improve comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model patent jury instructions and suggestions regarding instructions and verdict forms are provided; expert presentation techniques and court guidance matter.
